topics: Deployment decision criteria: hosted vs dedicated vs private
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-30 15:00 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Ava Martinez, Marcus Lee (Redwood); Samir Patel, Olivia Grant, Harold Kim (Zephyr)

00:00 Samir: Okay thanks everyone for taking the time. We wanted to walk through the POC scoping, specifically how we should evaluate hosted vs dedicated vs private for our fraud scoring pipelines.
00:10 Ava: Great, thanks Samir, yeah. I'll kick us off. Quick intros — I'm Ava, AE at Redwood, and Marcus is our solutions engineer.
00:18 Marcus: Hey everyone. Quick note, transcription may mangle some product names but we'll try to be clear.
00:25 Olivia: Just to frame, we have a few production constraints — sub-150ms 95th percentile on in-path scoring for checkout flows, and around 200 QPS for peak. Data residency has to be US-only and encryption at rest with customer-managed keys is a hard requirement.
00:42 Samir: Also cost is a factor — we expect to run hundreds of millions of tokens per month if this expands. So unit cost and predictable latency matter.
00:51 Marcus: Good, that's helpful. From a Redwood perspective there's three deployment profiles that map to those needs. Hosted API is fastest to get started, we manage infra, gives you streaming and autoscaling. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and lower unit cost at scale. Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you customer-managed network, KMS integration, and on-prem options for locked-down compliance.
01:18 Harold: Does hosted support CMEK — customer-managed encryption keys?
01:22 Marcus: Hosted can integrate with external KMS for Dedicated and Private obviously; hosted supports an encrypted tenant model but if strict CMEK is a requirement we typically recommend Dedicated or Private. There's been some confusion historically — the hosted offering supports envelope encryption but not direct HSM-backed customer key control.
01:40 Samir: Okay so that rules out hosted if CMEK is non-negotiable. But if we use hosted with strong envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key at the tenant level, is that acceptable for our auditors?
01:53 Harold: Our compliance team prefers direct KMS control, ideally HSM-backed. We need to confirm with auditors but lean toward Dedicated or Private.
02:05 Ava: Noted. For the POC we can still bench hosted to get latency/throughput numbers quickly, even if Dedicated/Private are the final target. It helps us baseline unit cost.
02:16 Olivia: Walk me through performance tradeoffs. If we need 150ms p95 at 200 QPS for a 1.5k token median sequence, what should we expect?
02:28 Marcus: Rough numbers — on hosted using a highly optimized quantized variant at ~1.5k seq, you're looking at median token latencies in the low single-digit ms range for the runtime but end-to-end p95 with network and cold-starts can be 100-250ms depending on batching. Dedicated with pinned capacity and warm KV-cache eliminates cold starts and gives tighter p95, often under 150ms at that QPS if you size GPUs appropriately. Private on-prem can be tuned further but depends heavily on customer infra (NICs, nvlink).
02:59 Samir: So Dedicated seems like the safest to meet p95 SLO. Is there a recommended sizing guideline?
03:06 Marcus: Yes — we usually start with a model of throughput: tokens per second per GPU depends on model size and quantization. For your workload ballpark, assuming a 13B model quantized to q4x2, a single A100-style GPU can handle around 4–6k tokens/s with good batching. So for 200 QPS at 1.5k tokens that's ~300k tokens/s peak, so you'd need on the order of 50–75 GPU-equivalents if you don't use batching and caching. But with aggressive batching and prefix caching (you mentioned many prompts share structure), we can reduce it materially — often 3–5x. We should run a bench with your real prompts to be sure.
03:55 Olivia: Wow okay that delta is big. We do have a lot of repeated prefixes.
04:00 Marcus: Exactly; Redwood's KV prefix caching can remove repeated compute for the shared prompt parts. For POC we want to capture realistic distribution: top N prompts, average token lengths, and 95th length.
04:14 Ava: Action item — Olivia to share sample prompt set and 72-hour traffic profile.
04:19 Olivia: Yep I'll get that over.
04:22 Samir: On benchmarks, we want both latency percentiles and cost per 1M tokens. Can you also show fallbacks and model variant routing? We may want a cheaper model for lower-sensitivity requests.
04:34 Marcus: Sure — for POC we'll run three experiments: hosted baseline on Redwood-hosted; dedicated with reserved pool sized for your 95th SLO; and a simulated private run (if you can provide infra metrics we can estimate). We'll capture p50/p95/p99, throughput, and cost per token for each. Also include multi-model routing tests.
04:54 Harold: For security we need audit logs, RBAC, SAML/SSO integration, and retention controls. Also need to understand where logs live for hosted.
05:03 Ava: Redwood Console exposes per-route logs, tracing hooks, and token-level cost — for hosted logs are encrypted and retained per tenant; for Dedicated/Private you get more control and can ship logs to your SIEM. We'll attach our SOC2 report and a security datasheet.
05:18 Harold: Great. Will you also provide evidence of penetration test cadence?
05:22 Marcus: Yes, we'll include PT summaries and a contact for the security questionnaire.
05:27 Samir: Timeline — what's typical for a POC and then ramp to production?
05:31 Ava: Typical POC is 3–6 weeks: week 0 onboarding + sample data sharing, week 1 hosted bench and tune, week 2 dedicated sizing and pilot, week 3 integration tests and security review. For Dedicated procurement lead times depend on reserved capacity — if you want committed GPUs we often see 4–8 weeks to provision in some regions. Private on-prem can be longer depending on infra.
05:55 Olivia: Does Redwood provide an on-prem appliance or just software?
06:00 Marcus: We ship a private package that can run in customer VPCs or on-prem; it requires Kubernetes and GPUs. We can support an air-gapped bundle for high-compliance environments.
06:10 Samir: For our success criteria we'll define three buckets: latency SLO (p95 < 150ms), inference cost target (< $X per 1M tokens — we'll supply target), and security criteria (CMEK/HSM, SOC2). If POC meets latency and security but unit cost is higher, we're willing to consider Dedicated to lower unit cost.
06:32 Ava: Perfect. We'll fold those into the POC success criteria doc.
06:36 Samir: Any known gotchas? For example, batching affecting tail latency?
06:40 Marcus: Yes batching is a double-edged sword. More batching increases throughput and lowers cost but can increase per-request latency variability. That's where smart routing and policy-based fallbacks help — you can route latency-sensitive requests to a lower-latency reserved pool and burst others to hosted cheaper capacity. We'll include those patterns in the POC.
06:59 Olivia: On cost modeling — can you provide a workbook with assumptions?
07:03 Ava: We'll include a pricing workbook and sensitivity analysis: tokens, QPS, batching factor, model variant mix.
07:09 Samir: For benchmarks please include warm vs cold start numbers and cache hit rates.
07:13 Marcus: Agreed. We'll run cold/warm experiments and measure KV-cache effectiveness.
07:17 Harold: Final security note — we may need to run a shadow traffic test in our environment before full cutover. Is that supported?
07:24 Marcus: Yes, that pattern is common — we can mirror traffic to a Dedicated pool in a test VPC. For hosted that's trickier but possible with a proxy.
07:33 Ava: Okay to recap: 1) Zephyr shares prompts and traffic profile; 2) Redwood runs hosted baseline benchmark; 3) Redwood drafts POC scope, pricing for Hosted/Dedicated/Private; 4) Security exchange SOC2 and KMS details; 5) Schedule follow-up for bench review next week.
07:50 Samir: Sounds good. One more question on SLA — if we go Dedicated can we get latency SLO in contract?
07:56 Ava: For Dedicated we can include SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in enterprise contracts; we'll flag this for legal.
08:04 Olivia: Thanks — we'll aim to get sample data to you by Jan 5th.
08:08 Marcus: Great, we'll queue the hosted bench as soon as we get samples.
08:12 Harold: I'll circulate the security Qs by Friday.
08:15 Ava: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the POC doc.
08:20 Meeting end.

Notes: transcript includes minor transcription artifacts; some product terms like "CMEK" and "KV-cache" may be spelled differently by the auto-transcriber.

Recap (verbatim style):
- Success criteria: p95 < 150ms, target cost per 1M tokens (customer to provide), CMEK/HSM + SOC2.
- Benchmarks to run: hosted baseline, dedicated sizing, simulated private estimate; measure p50/p95/p99, throughput, warm vs cold, cache hit rate, cost per token.
- Sizing: initial back-of-envelope indicates significant GPU requirement, but caching/batching expected to reduce needs by ~3–5x; real bench required.
- Timeline: POC 3–6 weeks; Dedicated provisioning 4–8 weeks; Private depends on infra.
